<reason>Both sides ran disciplined, genuinely engaged cases. CON's two best routes were (a) the instability of "primarily," sprung as a trap via Colston, and (b) the dilemma that if bronze-and-horse form cannot be defeated by text, the museum fails identically, so relocation is theatre. PRO neutralized the second, which was the load-bearing objection: the museum's frame is evidentiary rather than endorsing ("the building already won"; nobody reads a Klan robe in a vitrine as institutional approval), and PRO then tied that back to the concrete features of a square — plinth, sightline, renewed public maintenance in every citizen's name. CON's attempted answer ("the frame is whatever the city says") was both weaker and clipped, and PRO's closing turned it into a clean distinction between saying something about an object and doing something daily in everyone's name. On Colston, PRO's Royal African Company answer was plausible and substantive rather than evasive; CON's Washington-Jefferson extension was sharp but PRO's "honor rests on the trade's proceeds vs. founding a republic" line survived, and PRO fairly showed that annotation requires the same contested judgments (who gets a plaque, who writes it, which are left alone). CON scored real hits on practical reversibility (storage yards, no council re-erects) and on funding parity, and its "keep the argument, reject the rule" reframe was the best original move in the debate. But PRO's honor-versus-memory distinction, the finite-civic-honor framing, and the asymmetry-of-error weighing (a dead man's reputation vs. the child walking past) were left standing as reasons to prefer the motion, while CON's closing partly rested on characterizing the motion as forbidding deliberation, which PRO had already answered with "both sides must judge." Two clipped CON turns are a further execution cost.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's [A4.3]-[A4.4] answer to CON's either/or dilemma: the museum speaks in the voice of evidence rather than endorsement (the Klan robe in a vitrine), so the same object can teach more indoors while endorsing less — defusing CON's strongest structural objection, with CON's rejoinder both weaker and clipped.</best_rebuttal>
